newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW/Childrens B'casting turns to investors.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW/Childrens B'casting turns to investors.

text.p: Children's Broadcasting Corp, seeking a cash infusion to expand its child-oriented radio network, will seek to pique investor interest with a series of meetings in October.
"We've mailed out books (on the company) to potential investors, and there has been a lot of positive response," Christopher Dahl, chairman and chief executive officer, said in a telephone interview.
The company on Monday also will seek approval to increase its authorized shares to 50 million from 12.5 million.
The additional shares are not earmarked for any specific purpose, but Dahl noted that the Minneapolis-based company has made acquisitions for both stock and cash in the past.
Dahl said no equity offerings are planned, but the company may float debt.
Analyst John Vareka of John G. Kinnard said, "Children's Broadcasting doesn't have deep pockets. It needs capital to expand, possibly through a partnership or some kind of alliance."
In July, Children's Broadcasting hired Southcoast Capital Corp to help it explore ways to maximize shareholder value.
Analysts said Children's Broadcasting lost some momentum in July when ABC Radio Networks Inc terminated an operations agreement with the company.
To protect its position, Children's Broadcasting said Friday it sued ABC Radio and its parent, Walt Disney Co, for allegedly trying to copy its programming format.

Dahl said his company, with a network of 32 radio stations across the country, targets the pre-teen market. "This 20 percent (segment) of the country has never had a radio format directed at them. There's a huge marketing hole," he said.
"As much as I dislike what Disney and ABC are doing, it certainly validates the fact that somebody else feels it's a pretty important market overlooked for a long time," Dahl said.

Dahl said the company's main focus is to boost U.S. market penetration, which now stands at about 40 percent. It will do that by acquisitions in the top 10 markets and lining up affiliate stations to carry its Radio AAHS programming in secondary markets.
The company is negotiating with potential affiliates in 20 to 25 radio markets.
"We're looking at mid-40 percent (penetration) by the end of 1996 and 56 percent at the end of 1997," he said.
Increased penetration will give the company more access to advertisers who regularly spend $1 billion-plus a year.
Children's Broadcasting traded Friday at 5-1/4, off 1/8.
